extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing inventive step (obviousness) of patent claims across scenarios (similar/different prior art, selection inventions, numerical/parameter limitations, product-by-process, combination inventions). Covers evidentiary and reasoning standards, examples, and when advantageous effects rescue inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close similarity of a function, work, or operation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a close similarity in a function, work, or operation exists between a claimed invention and a cited invention or between cited inventions, there can be a well-founded ground that a person skilled in the art would have arrived at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether functions/operations are essentially identical across claimed and cited inventions; if so, applying features from one to another is deemed obvious to a person skilled in the art. Example: filtering apparatuses for different applications sharing identical function/operation — combining filtering part from one to the other is obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close relation of technical fields
rubrics_metrics.description: A publicly known technical means for solving the technical problem of the claimed invention in a related technical field can be a strong ground for considering that a person skilled in the art could have achieved the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If technical fields are related (e.g., gloves and socks), known solutions in one field may be obvious to apply to the other. Examiner should consider related-field knowledge and whether application would be easy for the skilled person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness despite different problem if easy via ordinary creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a cited invention addresses a different problem, if it is obvious that a person skilled in the art can easily arrive at the claimed invention through a mere exercise of ordinary creativity, the inventive step can be denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether combining teachings from differently‑problematic prior art would require inventive skill or merely ordinary creativity. Example: adapting grooves from a metal disk brake (dust removal) to a carbon disc brake (prevent water attachment) may be an obvious combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere exercise of ordinary creativity of a person skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Common improvements based on general applications of known art, reasoning based on known physical properties, or referring to other technical fields to solve a known problem fall into ordinary creativity and typically negate inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes selecting optimal material from known materials, optimizing numerical ranges, replacing with equivalents, workshop modification of design, partial removal of features, and simple change of use. If differences between claimed and cited inventions fall only into these categories, inventive step is usually denied unless another ground supports it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacement with equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitution of a known feature with another known feature that has the same function and is an equivalent is not considered inventive if it fails to exhibit an unexpected advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To treat a substitution as ordinary creativity, it should be justifiable that the replacement was obvious at filing and that the substitute was known as an equivalent before filing. Examiner may submit evidence that features were known equivalents. Examples: replacing SiC with Aluminum if known equivalent; substituting magnesium carbonate for magnesium oxide if known conversion occurs under conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop modification of a design in applying a specific technology
rubrics_metrics.description: When an invention can be merely arrived at by applying normal design procedures without affecting the technical concept of prior art and shows no advantageous effects, the inventive step cannot be acknowledged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences due solely to selection of parameters (size, proportion, relative dimensions, amounts) from a limited range are typically non-inventive. However, if such changes produce unexpected functional or reactive changes with advantageous effects, inventive step may be acknowledged. Examples: modifying protrusion sizes or positions for a microwave door may be obvious; but replacing sealing material with heat insulation that prevents freezing may show inventive step if effect is demonstrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial removal of technical features
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is not considered inventive if omission of some technical features known in the prior art simply removes the related function/effect and is obvious to the skilled person; but inventive step may be acknowledged when omission does not affect or enhances function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether omission merely removes functionality or whether it unexpectedly improves or leaves function intact. Example: omitting a water-soluble silicate from toothpaste to cut cost removes the protective effect and is non-inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple change and limitation of use of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that merely changes the use of a known invention, or imposes a simple further restriction of such use without exhibiting any advantage, is not considered inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a new use is naturally expected from prior properties (e.g., reusing synthetic oil as cutting oil because its lubricating properties change slowly), inventive step is negated.

rubrics_metrics.name: General application of known art
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a known technique in a closely analogous situation to solve a prior-art problem with readily anticipated effect is not inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If application of a known technique leads to unexpected beneficial effects in combination with other components, inventive step may be acknowledged. Examples: transforming a conventional formulation to liquid form may be non-inventive if common practice; forming a leak-detecting hole in a pipe joint if commonly practiced is non-inventive; using an already-prevailing component type (e.g., ball grid array) for trays is non-inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantageous effects to be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: If an effect derived from matters defining a claimed invention is advantageous compared to a cited invention, it supports affirmatively the inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarkable advantageous effects not foreseeable by a skilled person from the state of the art can rebut a prima facie obviousness finding. Particularly important in unpredictable fields (selection inventions, chemical). Examiner may rely on inventor's assertions and experimental evidence if the effect is inferable from the description and drawings; unsupported assertions should not be considered. Case law references cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining inventive step of a selection invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A selection invention selects a more specific concept from a generic concept disclosed in cited art; selecting an optimized concept experimentally is usually ordinary creativity unless the selection generates advantageous effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For inventive step to be acknowledged, all specific concepts in the selection should yield qualitatively different or quantitatively prominent advantageous effects compared to the cited invention. The detailed description should explain the advantageous effect; experimental confirmation is not strictly required but may be submitted if effects are doubted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining inventive step of an invention including numerical limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental selection of an optimal numerical range from known art is normally ordinary creativity; inventive step is possible if the limited numerical range produces a remarkably improved effect across the boundary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria for significance: (1) significance required regarding any part of range if claimed invention is a continuation of cited invention; (2) if inventions solve different problems with qualitatively different effects, significance is not required. To acknowledge significance, there must be a remarkable change across the boundary and (a) technical meaning of the numerical limitation described in detail, and (b) embodiments or supplemental materials proving the range is critical—ideally objective experimental results covering the range. Examples given where numeric limits without explanation are technically meaningless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining inventive step of a parameter invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A parameter invention introduces a non-standard parameter (mathematical correlation of parameters) as an essential element; inventive-step determination must consider the technical meaning and function caused by the parameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First determine subject matter from description/drawings/common knowledge. If the parameter is merely a different expression or weakly linked to effect, inventive step denied. If parameter functions like a numerical limitation, those criteria apply. Examiner may raise reasonable doubt and must state grounds concretely; if parameter is standard/common, these special criteria are not applied. Also, if converting measurement/definitions makes claimed and cited inventions similar, novelty/inventive step may be lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining inventive step of a product invention described by its manufacturing process
rubrics_metrics.description: When a product is claimed by a manufacturing method, the examiner should determine inventive step by comparing the product itself (composition/properties) with publicly known products, not by considering the manufacturing method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The object to be protected is the product itself; the manufacturing method/apparatus need not be considered for novelty/inventive-step assessment. If the product shows remarkable property changes due to the method (demonstrated in description), inventive step may be acknowledged based on product characteristics. Examples provided (seat-belt belt coupling, cannaf tea inorganic content).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of the inventive step of a combination invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination invention gathers technical features disclosed in prior art as a whole to solve a technical problem; inventive step shall not be negated merely because each element is individually known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine inventive step by considering the technical idea and structural combination as a whole, including difficulty in combining elements and unique effects of the whole. Combining multiple disclosures is permissible only if a skilled person could easily combine them at filing; examiner should consider motivation/hints in cited inventions, state of the art, common general knowledge, technical trends and industry demands. Well‑known and commonly‑used art definitions provided. Number of prior art disclosures to be combined is not specially limited, but ease of combination is critical. Example: separating download of game program and game data may be considered obvious depending on technical difference and context.
